bridges.mechanism: Stepped‑up enforcement actions (inspections, seizures, interdictions) raise the probability of escalation and sudden trade disruptions, prompting rapid repositioning and higher realized volatility in Treasury and related markets.

A reduction in crude and refined product throughput through key chokepoints directly increases shortages and rerouting pressure for fuel and bunker supply chains used to sustain military and logistical operations supporting the Ukraine war, raising critical‑supply risk.

A sustained increase in oil transit volumes eases near‑term supply concerns, lowers upside inflation and geopolitical risk premia priced into long‑dated sovereign bonds, and so reduces long‑term yields.

A sustained reduction in oil transit volume pushes up fuel and transport costs, hurting energy‑intensive sectors and regional employers who then press policymakers for protective trade actions or relief, raising domestic political pressure.

Acute reductions in oil transit volume drive up regional fuel and electricity prices and can cause localized fuel shortages, forcing temporary curtailment or higher operating costs at energy‑intensive datacenters and fabs and thereby reducing available compute.

An increase in naval escorts and active maritime security in response to Iran pressure lowers transit risk for weapons and aid shipments and thereby facilitates higher rates of military and materiel transfers to Ukraine; conversely, a drop in security suppresses those flows.

A sharp rise in shipping insurance and war‑risk premia for vessels in the Iran‑affected sea lanes immediately raises transport costs, forces rerouting and hedging, and triggers price and volatility spikes in energy, grain and commodity markets linked to the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

A rapid rise in shipping war‑risk and insurance premia acts as a high‑frequency signal of elevated geopolitical risk that causes immediate repricing across fixed‑income desks and increases trade volumes into/out of Treasuries, raising intramarket price swings.

A sharp rise in shipping insurance and war‑risk premia immediately raises landed import prices and delivery uncertainty for firms and consumers, spurring industry and constituency lobbying for protective or compensatory trade measures that increase domestic political pressure on governments.

Rising war‑risk and hull insurance premia raise the cost and risk of maritime transport for high‑value semiconductor tools, substrates and chemicals, prompting delays, cancellations or reduced frequency of shipments that create immediate throughput bottlenecks at fabs.

Elevated vulnerability of logistics and energy infrastructure raises the risk of sudden systemic shocks and liquidity stress, prompting monetary authorities to increase long‑dated bond buybacks to stabilize yields and market functioning.

Rising susceptibility of logistics, energy, and industrial systems to strikes accelerates adoption of AI-driven monitoring, predictive maintenance, and automation as firms and governments deploy solutions to preserve operations and resilience.

Sustained increases in Western military and materiel support to Ukraine divert naval assets, patrol rotations, and ISR resources away from the Middle East, reducing aggregate maritime security presence and interdiction capacity in key sea lanes.
Large, sustained external military and fiscal assistance programs trigger supplemental appropriations and financing decisions that increase scheduled sovereign debt issuance to cover support costs.

Large, visible increases in US/Canadian military and financial support for Ukraine generate domestic scrutiny and constituency demands to prioritize or protect local industries, raising pressure on leaders to take tariff or trade-positioning actions in the bilateral dispute.

Sustained large-scale military and economic assistance programs mobilize public procurement and signal elevated geopolitical risk, prompting private and public investors to direct additional capital toward defense- and dual-use AI platforms and infrastructure in US/allied markets.

Heightened volatility in commodity and freight markets tied to the Russia–Ukraine war raises perceived systemic risk for tanker and merchant routes, prompting insurers to widen war‑risk and hull/policy premia for ships operating in regions where Iran exerts pressure.

Volatility and functional strains in commodity, insurance and related markets produce margin calls, forced reallocations and cross-market spillovers that directly amplify price swings in the Treasury market.

Heightened commodity and financial volatility tied to the conflict increases investor risk aversion and liquidity constraints, producing a measurable short-term pullback in venture and institutional funding into AI startups and projects.

Disruptions and sanctions on Russian crude prompt buyers to source more oil from Gulf producers, increasing tanker throughput through chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and raising measured oil transit volume.
Acute disruptions to energy and key commodity supplies raise near-term inflation expectations and term premia, forcing repricing of long-dated sovereign bonds upward.

War-driven interruptions to critical inputs and energy prompt North American manufacturers to regionalize and re-source components away from fragile cross-border chains, directly reducing depth of US–Canada industrial integration.

War-related disruptions and sanctions interrupt supplies of key semiconductor inputs (e.g., specialty gases, substrates, tool shipments) and constrain cross-border equipment flows, forcing fabs to idle or cut throughput and reducing near-term advanced chip output.

Higher applied tariffs on US–Canada trade raise costs and customs frictions for cross‑border production and logistics, producing delays and lower volumes of military equipment and dual‑use shipments from North American suppliers destined for Ukraine.

A rise in applied bilateral tariff rates abruptly changes import prices and corporate profit outlooks and triggers rapid portfolio rebalancing and liquidity shifts, producing larger and more frequent price swings in the treasury market.

Stronger reciprocal tariff measures by Canada lead Ottawa to adopt legal protections, guidance, or financial support that enable Canadian and allied firms to keep trading with sanctioned Iranian entities, which reduces third-party firms' willingness to comply with U.S. secondary sanctions.

Higher reciprocal retaliation broadens and prolongs trade disruptions and import-price pass-through, lifting inflation expectations and risk/term premia and thereby putting upward pressure on long-term sovereign bond yields.

Greater reliance on the bilateral partner for critical inputs magnifies the real-economy impact of tariff moves, causing faster revisions to growth and cash-flow forecasts that translate into larger intraday and cross-market volatility in treasuries.

A breakdown in deep US–Canada manufacturing integration severs just‑in‑time lines for components (electronics, ammunition subcomponents, vehicle parts) used in Western supplies to Ukraine, directly increasing the risk of shortages and rerouting failures in those critical supply chains.

Disruption of integrated US–Canada supply and maintenance chains delays delivery of spare parts, repair crews and specialist equipment used for energy and logistics infrastructure relevant to Ukraine’s sustainment, increasing susceptibility to outages and cascading failures.

Deep US‑Canada manufacturing integration means tariffs or border frictions disrupt delivery of servers, power equipment and specialized components for North American data centers, delaying builds and expansions and reducing available AI training/inference compute capacity in the near term.

A material rise in long-term sovereign yields increases governments' near-term debt-service costs and borrowing needs, squeezing fiscal space and prompting delays, scaling back, or re-prioritization of planned military and financial assistance to Ukraine.

Sustained rises in long-term sovereign yields raise financing costs and reduce export competitiveness for interest‑sensitive industries, prompting policymakers to raise applied tariff rates to shield affected domestic producers or to generate revenue to offset higher borrowing costs.

A rise in long-term sovereign yields raises the required return and discount rates for long-duration tech projects, directly reducing venture, private-equity and datacenter financing commitments into AI infrastructure and startups.

Large scheduled government debt issuance competes for bank and capital-market funding and prompts export-credit and commercial lenders to reprioritize balance-sheet capacity, delaying or downsizing financing for capital-intensive wafer fabs and slowing chip capacity expansions.

A reduction in official long-dated bond buybacks increases term-premia and funding volatility for long-dated corporate debt, making lenders and project financiers more reluctant to underwrite multi-year datacenter and GPU-accelerator buildouts, modestly slowing additions to compute capacity.

Sharp spikes in Treasury-market volatility force insurers and reinsurers to de‑risk and reprice exposures, reducing war‑risk capacity and driving up war‑risk and hull insurance premia for vessels operating in the Gulf/Strait of Hormuz.

Sharp Treasury-market volatility triggers risk-off behavior by asset managers and creates political pressure on legislators and ministries to shore up domestic markets, causing donor states and private contractors to slow or defer shipments and financing for Ukraine.

Elevated volatility in Treasury and related fixed-income markets leads banks and insurers to withdraw or repricing trade finance and war-risk insurance, raising the likelihood of interrupted deliveries of fuel, spare parts and munitions into Ukraine.

Sharp increases in Treasury-market volatility produce visible losses for pension funds, money-market stress and sudden credit tightening for exporters and manufacturers, which quickly raises domestic business and voter demands for protectionist measures and therefore heightens political pressure to impose tariffs.

Spikes in fixed-income and related market volatility trigger risk-off behaviour at hyperscalers and corporate IT buyers, causing procurement freezes, contract renegotiations and postponed rollouts that reduce the short-term rate of AI model deployments.

A noticeable drop in perceived fiscal credibility weakens other actors' belief in the durability and political will behind US sanctions, leading banks and traders to lower voluntary compliance and increase tolerance for secondary exposure to Iranian counterparties.

A demonstrable improvement in perceived fiscal credibility eases fears of fiscal collapse and reduces calls for protective, revenue‑raising trade measures, thereby lowering domestic political pressure to pursue tariffs against the bilateral partner.

An expansion of US aggregate AI compute (more domestic datacenter and accelerator supply) directly substitutes for imported compute services and specialized hardware from Canadian providers, reducing the bilateral share of critical compute-related imports.

An increase in advanced chip manufacturing capacity globally reduces scarcity of specialized components used in drones, guidance and comms, lowering the exposure of conflict-relevant supply chains to interruption or rerouting.

Policies and large public subsidies to expand domestic advanced chip capacity (driven by US–China rivalry) raise expected government outlays and future debt supply, pressuring long-term yields higher as markets price increased fiscal financing needs.

A rapid increase in US domestic advanced chip capacity is typically accompanied by industrial-policy measures (local-content rules, procurement preferences and safeguard tariffs) that raise applied import tariffs on competing semiconductor inputs and finished goods from trading partners, including Canada.

Increased investment into AI specifically funds rapid procurement and fielding of maritime surveillance and autonomous response platforms by private security firms and state actors, raising on‑water detection and response capacity.

A surge in private capital into AI projects diverts demand from safe sovereign bonds, raising Treasury yields and liquidity strains that increase the likelihood and scale of official buyback interventions to stabilize long-dated yields.

A surge of US investment into AI creates new domestic corporate and investor constituencies that quickly lobby policymakers for protective trade measures against foreign competitors, increasing domestic political pressure to take tariff or barrier actions in the US–Canada relationship.

Improved AI model capability speeds and sharpens analysis of commercial satellite, AIS and RF data used by navies and commercial monitors, prompting more frequent and effective surveillance and interdiction in key choke points.

Higher aggregate AI model capability yields improved automated target recognition, sensor fusion, and mission-planning tools that adversaries can use to find, prioritize and prosecute economic/civilian infrastructure targets faster and at higher tempo.

Rapid improvements in deployed AI models enable more aggressive, model-driven trading strategies and automated rebalancing that amplify order flow and create larger, more frequent price swings in the Treasury market.

Faster operational deployment of AI into port inspection, cargo screening and trade‑monitoring workflows enables authorities to detect and act on sanction-evasive shipments more frequently and rigorously.

Faster, broader operational deployment of AI into logistics, industrial control and energy management systems increases automated dependencies and attack surface, making economic infrastructure more susceptible to cascading outages from kinetic or cyber incidents tied to the conflict.

Faster operational deployment of AI in US manufacturing and logistics prompts reshoring and vertical integration (automation replacing cross-border tasks), directly reducing the depth of Canada–US cross-border manufacturing and value-chain ties.

Sanctions scope
nodes.description: The breadth of sanction measures applied extraterritorially, measured by the range of economic sectors, actors and transactions targeted.

nodes.label: Enforcement intensity
nodes.description: The rigor and frequency of enforcement actions and compliance checks applied to implement sanctions.

nodes.label: Third‑party compliance rate
nodes.description: The aggregated propensity of external economic actors and intermediaries to comply with or acquiesce to secondary sanctions.

nodes.label: Sanctions circumvention activity
nodes.description: The volume and sophistication of activities and networks used to evade or bypass sanctions (e.g., reflagging, front entities, opaque transactions).

nodes.label: Oil transit volume
nodes.description: The throughput of crude oil and refined products transiting the principal maritime chokepoints measured as volume per time.

nodes.label: Global oil supply balance
nodes.description: The net balance between global oil supply and demand that determines headroom and sensitivity to regional disruptions.

nodes.label: Maritime security level
nodes.description: The aggregate level of naval and security presence, surveillance and interdiction capability in key sea lanes.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance premia
nodes.description: The price level of insurance and war-risk premia charged for commercial shipping operating in the affected maritime regions.

nodes.label: Vessel transit delay rate
nodes.description: The rate of additional delays, rerouting and time-in-transit experienced by commercial vessels in response to risk or restrictions.

nodes.label: Market volatility level
nodes.description: The amplitude of price and return volatility across energy, equity and credit markets tied to regional risk perceptions.

nodes.label: Investor risk positioning
nodes.description: The aggregate directional exposure and hedging stance of investors to assets sensitive to regional sanctions and conflict.

nodes.label: Trade‑hub dependency
nodes.description: The degree to which intermediary trade and finance hubs depend on trade flows and services that are vulnerable to sanctions pressure.

nodes.label: Financial channel connectivity
nodes.description: The strength and opacity of banking, payments and alternative financial channels linking the targeted economy to global markets.

nodes.label: Politico‑military escalation pressure
nodes.description: The internal and external pressures on decision makers that raise the propensity to employ military or coercive responses.

nodes.label: Energy market liquidity
nodes.description: The depth and immediacy with which energy commodity markets can absorb trades without large price dislocations.

nodes.label: Diplomatic coordination
nodes.description: The degree of aligned diplomatic posture and cooperative action among external actors regarding sanctions, mediation or de‑escalation.

Military capability
nodes.description: The aggregate level of available offensive and defensive military resources, platforms and operational readiness.

nodes.label: Economic target strike rate
nodes.description: The frequency and intensity of kinetic strikes explicitly aimed at economic and civilian infrastructure per unit time.

nodes.label: Economic infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of logistics, energy, industrial and commercial facilities to damage, outage and cascading failure.

nodes.label: Logistics network resilience
nodes.description: The capacity of transport, storage and distribution networks to maintain function and recover from disruptions.

nodes.label: Air defense effectiveness
nodes.description: The probability and rate at which air defenses detect, track and successfully intercept incoming aerial threats.

nodes.label: Political mobilization
nodes.description: The degree of domestic political support, mobilization willingness and legitimacy for wartime policies and measures.

nodes.label: International support flow
nodes.description: The rate and volume of external transfers of military equipment, funding, intelligence and advisory assistance.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure
nodes.description: The intensity and economic impact of externally imposed trade, financial and transaction restrictions.

nodes.label: Defense industry output
nodes.description: The production and delivery rate of weapons, munitions, air‑defense systems and related military materiel.

nodes.label: Information warfare intensity
nodes.description: The scale, reach and effectiveness of coordinated messaging, influence operations, cyber operations and propaganda.

nodes.label: Market disruption
nodes.description: The level of volatility and functional disruption in financial, insurance and commodity markets linked to the conflict.

nodes.label: Civilian casualty rate
nodes.description: The rate at which noncombatant deaths and injuries occur as a result of military operations and strikes.

nodes.label: Legal control over infrastructure
nodes.description: The extent and scope of legal authorities to seize, operate, restrict or compel use of critical infrastructure assets.

nodes.label: Cross-border weapon flow
nodes.description: The rate of movement of arms, munitions and dual‑use materiel across borders and through illicit channels.

nodes.label: Critical supply risk
nodes.description: The exposure of key material, component and energy supply chains to interruption, scarcity or rerouting.

nodes.label: Public support for external aid
nodes.description: The level of public opinion in external societies favoring provision of military, financial or humanitarian assistance.

Escalating US–Canada Trade War Over Tariffs
Average applied tariff rate
nodes.description: The weighted average level of import tariffs applied on goods crossing the bilateral border.

nodes.label: Retaliatory reciprocity degree
nodes.description: The extent to which tariff actions are met with proportional reciprocal measures by the counterparty.

nodes.label: Trade policy uncertainty
nodes.description: The perceived unpredictability of future trade measures and the risk of sudden policy shifts affecting bilateral trade.

nodes.label: Negotiation intensity
nodes.description: The frequency, urgency and scope of active policy negotiations addressing bilateral trade disputes.

nodes.label: Supply-chain disruption level
nodes.description: The accumulated degree of interruptions, delays and capacity shortfalls in cross-border supply chains.

nodes.label: Bilateral goods flow
nodes.description: The volume and value rate of goods moving across the bilateral border per unit time.

nodes.label: Financial market volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude of short-term price fluctuations in equity, bond and derivative markets linked to the dispute.

nodes.label: Currency volatility
nodes.description: The variability of the bilateral exchange rate and short-term currency movements associated with the trade conflict.

nodes.label: Commodity price pressure
nodes.description: The upward or downward pressure on prices of key traded commodities (metals, energy, agricultural) driven by trade actions.

nodes.label: Investor risk sentiment
nodes.description: The degree to which investors reprice risk for assets exposed to bilateral trade disruption and policy uncertainty.

nodes.label: Corporate investment commitment
nodes.description: The aggregated level of firms' planned capital expenditures and location decisions affected by bilateral trade conditions.

nodes.label: Supply-chain reconfiguration rate
nodes.description: The pace at which firms alter sourcing, production locations or logistics to reduce exposure to the bilateral partner.

nodes.label: Import dependence
nodes.description: The share of critical inputs and finished goods that the economy sources from the bilateral partner, indicating structural reliance.

nodes.label: Domestic political pressure
nodes.description: The intensity of domestic political demands on decision-makers to take protective or retaliatory trade actions.

nodes.label: Multilateral rule constraint
nodes.description: The strength and enforceability of international trade rules and dispute-resolution mechanisms constraining unilateral measures.

nodes.label: Industrial interdependence
nodes.description: The depth of cross-border integration in manufacturing and value chains that transmits shocks between economies.

nodes.label: Bond-market panic: Treasury buybacks, rising yields, and shaken credibility
Long-term bond yields
nodes.description: The prevailing interest rates on long-dated sovereign bonds that signal borrowing costs and discount rates for long-duration assets.

nodes.label: Government debt outstanding
nodes.description: The total stock of government debt securities outstanding that must be financed or rolled over over time.

nodes.label: Scheduled debt issuance
nodes.description: The rate and timing of planned government debt issuance entering the market over a given period.

nodes.label: Buyback intervention rate
nodes.description: The pace and scale of official market purchases of long-dated bonds intended to influence prices and yields.

nodes.label: Market liquidity depth
nodes.description: The ease with which large bond positions can be transacted without materially moving prices, measured by depth and bid-ask rawness.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: The magnitude and frequency of price swings in fixed-income and related markets reflecting uncertainty and repricing events.

nodes.label: Investor policy expectations
nodes.description: Market beliefs about future effectiveness and direction of fiscal and debt-management actions that shape trading and positioning.

nodes.label: Perceived fiscal credibility
nodes.description: The market's confidence in the fiscal authority's commitment and ability to manage debt, deficits, and financing plans.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: The additional yield investors require for holding longer-duration sovereign bonds relative to expected short rates.

nodes.label: Leverage and margin exposure
nodes.description: The aggregate level of borrowed funding and margin positions across leveraged market participants that amplify moves.

nodes.label: Cross-market capital flows
nodes.description: The net movement of capital between sovereign bonds, equities, currencies, commodities, and other asset classes.

nodes.label: Safe-haven demand
nodes.description: The intensity and speed of investor reallocations into perceived low-risk assets in response to stress or uncertainty.

nodes.label: Risk-asset allocation tilt
nodes.description: The net directional shift of portfolios toward or away from risk assets (equities, credit, EM) relative to bonds/cash.

nodes.label: Currency exchange pressure
nodes.description: The directional stress on major currency exchange rates caused by capital flows, yield differentials, and market sentiment.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied and survey-based forecasts of future inflation that influence real yields, term premia, and policy views.

nodes.label: Market structure resilience
nodes.description: The capacity of trading infrastructure, settlement plumbing, and regulatory backstops to absorb shocks and maintain orderly markets.

nodes.label: Potential tap of Treasury General Account to fund buybacks
Regulatory probes into Situational Awareness and banks
Forced deleveraging, redemptions and portfolio unwinds
AI‑infrastructure race fuels market, industrial and geopolitical disruption
Compute capacity
nodes.description: Total available AI training and inference compute (e.g., aggregate FLOPS and usable accelerators) accessible across the system.

nodes.label: Advanced chip manufacturing capacity
nodes.description: Global production capability for specialized AI chips and related silicon (measured as throughput or maximum wafer-equivalent output).

nodes.label: AI server inventory
nodes.description: Quantity of deployable servers, GPU/accelerator racks, and supporting hardware available for AI infrastructure deployment.

nodes.label: AI capital flow
nodes.description: Rate at which investment capital (equity, debt, M&A funding) is entering AI infrastructure, platforms, and related ventures.

nodes.label: AI model capability
nodes.description: Aggregate performance, scale, and capability level of deployed and under-development AI models across the ecosystem.

nodes.label: Data availability
nodes.description: Volume, diversity, and accessibility of labeled and unlabeled data usable for training and operating AI systems.

nodes.label: AI talent supply
nodes.description: Available pool of skilled personnel (researchers, engineers, operators) qualified to build and run advanced AI systems.

nodes.label: Cloud capacity utilization
nodes.description: Fraction of cloud and hyperscaler capacity currently consumed by AI workloads versus available headroom.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain disruption risk
nodes.description: Probability and intensity of interruptions in logistics and component flows that affect AI hardware and infrastructure availability.

nodes.label: Export control tightness
nodes.description: Restrictiveness and enforcement intensity of trade and export controls that constrain cross-border flows of AI hardware and tech.

nodes.label: Cyber attack rate
nodes.description: Frequency and intensity of cyber intrusions, data breaches, and adversarial operations targeting AI infrastructure and datasets.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: Level and assertiveness of regulatory oversight, investigations, and compliance enforcement focused on AI products and markets.

nodes.label: Market concentration
nodes.description: Degree to which AI infrastructure, platforms, and key inputs are dominated by a small number of large providers.

nodes.label: Server price change rate
nodes.description: Rate of price change (upward or downward) for servers, accelerators, memory, and other critical AI hardware components.

nodes.label: Public trust in AI
nodes.description: Aggregate level of public and user confidence or distrust in AI systems and their real-world deployments.

nodes.label: AI operational deployment rate
nodes.description: Speed and volume at which AI models and autonomous systems are being put into production and real-world use cases.
